desc:
The string word consists of decimal digits (leading zeros are allowed). For every prefix of word, read it as a decimal number. Return an array flags of the same length as word where flags[i] is 1 if the number formed by word[0..i] is divisible by m, and 0 otherwise.

The prefixes can be thousands of digits long, so they cannot be converted to machine integers.

Example: word = "9210", m = 3: the prefixes are 9, 92, 921, 9210, of which 9, 921 and 9210 are multiples of 3, so the answer is [1, 0, 1, 1].
hints: Testing each prefix from scratch costs O(n) per prefix and the numbers are huge.
Going from prefix P to the next prefix gives the number P * 10 + digit.

You only need the remainder: rem = (rem * 10 + digit) % m is the remainder of the new prefix, because remainders respect addition and multiplication. A prefix is divisible exactly when its remainder is 0.
editorial: Keep rem, the remainder of the current prefix modulo m. Appending a digit transforms the number P into 10P + d, and modular arithmetic gives (10P + d) mod m = (10 (P mod m) + d) mod m. So one pass with a single running remainder answers every prefix.

The intermediate value rem * 10 + d is below 1010, which exceeds 32 bits, so use 64-bit integers in languages without arbitrary precision. Total time is O(n) and the output has one entry per character. Note that a prefix like "000" is the number 0, which is divisible by every m.
solution:
def divisiblePrefixes(word, m):
    rem = 0
    out = []
    for ch in word:
        rem = (rem * 10 + ord(ch) - 48) % m
        out.append(1 if rem == 0 else 0)
    return out
